rubrics_metrics.name: Historical criteria for governmental censorship (Milton's account)
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically magistrates and authorities took notice mainly of writings that were either blasphemous and atheistical, or libellous; other sects and opinions tending to voluptuousness were generally not prosecuted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton provides examples (Protagoras, Roman and Greek practices) to argue that legitimate suppression historically focused on blasphemy and defamation, not general censorship of all dissenting or licentious works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three principal criteria for sincere praise
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three principal things without which all praising is but courtship and flattery: (1) when that only is praised which is solidly worth praise; (2) when greatest likelihoods are brought that such things are truly and really in those persons to whom they are ascribed; (3) when he who praises, by showing that such his actual persuasion is of whom he writes, can demonstrate that he flatters not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton uses this tripartite test to evaluate genuine commendation vs. flattery; he applies it to political praise and to his own acquittal for extolling the Parliament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader self-sufficiency principle (Milton's advice)
rubrics_metrics.description: READ ANY BOOKS WHATEVER COME TO THY HANDS, FOR THOU ART SUFFICIENT BOTH TO JUDGE ARIGHT AND TO EXAMINE EACH MATTER.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton argues that mature readers are sufficient to judge and examine books themselves; he invokes scripture and tradition to support the view that exposure to many works is necessary for judgement and virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary harm from books: contagion/infection risk (Milton)
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the harms commonly feared from books is 'the infection that may spread' from them—i.e., the spread of corrupting or dangerous ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton argues this risk is often overstated, noting that religious controversies and even the Bible contain material that could be construed as infective, and that learned men are more at risk than the ignorant; he uses this to challenge the effectiveness of licensing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing as counterproductive to learning (Milton's conclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Licensing books (requiring prior approval) 'will be primely to the discouragement of all learning, and the stop of truth' by disexercising abilities and hindering discovery in religious and civil wisdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton traces licensing to the Inquisition and papal practice and argues it is historically associated with tyranny and suppression rather than with effective suppression of sedition or scandalous works.
